extracted.intended_audience: researchers and engineers working on neural theorem proving, formal theorem proving, and machine-learning-driven proof automation
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, releasing, and evaluating a cross-system dataset (miniF2F) of manually formalized Olympiad-level mathematical problem statements for benchmarking neural and automated theorem provers across multiple formal systems. Includes dataset composition, formalization guidelines, evaluation metrics, and baseline experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-system benchmark / unified dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: miniF2F: a dataset of formal Olympiad-level mathematics problem statements intended to provide a unified cross-system benchmark for neural theorem proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets Metamath, Lean, Isabelle (partially) and HOL Light (partially); drawn from AIME, AMC, IMO, and high-school/undergraduate sources to allow comparison of provers across different formal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-to-end verifiability (formal-to-formal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agent must receive IMO problems written in a formal mathematical format, and must produce a formal (i.e. machine-checkable) proof for that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark is end-to-end verifiable: produced proofs can be checked by the target proof assistant; proofs attached to statements are optional but evaluation requires machine-checkable proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of difficulty levels
rubrics_metrics.description: miniF2F spans a wide range of difficulty, centering around Olympiad-level problems and including problems sampled from the MATH dataset stratified by difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems are selected to cover difficulty levels 1–5 from MATH and Olympiad problems; the dataset includes both test and validation sets stratified to equally cover problem type and difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressibility constraint / subject focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements are chosen to be expressible in most formal systems, leading to a systemic focus on algebra, number theory and inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometry and combinatorial problems are less covered because they are generally challenging to formalize; the dataset prefers problems that do not require defining new mathematical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual formalization requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statements in miniF2F are all manually formalized and selected to cover a variety of difficulty levels for both humans and machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal proofs for these statements are optionally attached (i.e., attached proofs are not required for a statement to be part of the benchmark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset split methodology (stratified random split)
rubrics_metrics.description: miniF2F comprises a test set and a validation set, which are a stratified random split from the statements we formalized such that each set equally covers each problem type and difficulty (when available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 shows distribution; the split is intended to ensure comparable coverage across types and difficulty between validation and test sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versioning stability and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Versioning miniF2F is an evolving effort; the current version is v1 and the set of statements of each version is guaranteed to remain stable, only allowing fixes in case errors are later discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results should indicate the miniF2F version used; new statements will be added over time but frozen versions are used for reported evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of engagement and citation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no formal process to submit evaluation results; researchers are invited to cite miniF2F indicating the version used in their evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers are encouraged to contribute proofs found by their approaches back to the benchmark repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing aligned with target theorem prover libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of the benchmark associated with each theorem prover are meant to be licensed in a way aligned with the theorem prover’s main library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Metamath version released under the MIT License; Lean and Isabelle versions released under the Apache License.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability handling: multiple-choice problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-choice questions are generally straightforwardly formalizable by reformulating the statement using the right answer only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be fair in a competitive setup, formalize all possible choices and run provers on all of them, attributing points only if a proof of the correct answer is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability handling: word problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Word problems where significant information is presented in natural language generally require non-trivial effort to formalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically formalize by explicitly modeling the mathematical concepts and expressions while attempting to preserve the original mathematical difficulty; if formalization dominates difficulty, the problem may be discarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability handling: find-all / witness problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that require explicitifying a set or witness (e.g., 'find all ... such that ...') are not directly formalizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate by formalizing the statement with the provided witness/answer, turning the exercise into proving the correctness (and if needed uniqueness) of that answer—recognizing this may be an easier exercise and a limitation for fair human-vs-automated comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion: avoid problems requiring new concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Olympiad-type problems are of particular interest because the theories required to solve them are well identified and they generally do not require the definition of new mathematical concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property makes them suitable for cross-system comparisons because statements are expressible in multiple proof assistants without adding new foundational definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pass@N evaluation metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Pass@N where N is the number of proof search attempts per statement; Pass@N is computed by running more attempts per statement, averaged to get an unbiased, low-variance estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass@1, Pass@8 reported in experiments; Pass@N reflects probability of finding a valid proof within N independent attempts (averaging procedure as described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report average proof length
rubrics_metrics.description: Report average proof length across proofs found in each experimental run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables report mean proof length per system/model combination to characterize difficulty and verbosity of formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof search budget and baseline parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental runs specify search budgets and baseline parameters (e.g., 128 expansions budget; GPT-f attempts e = 16 tactics per expansion; tidy baseline attempts e = 17; tidy baseline parameters ωmax, dmax, imax, qmax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tidy baseline behavior described: when Q’s size reach qmax, candidate tactic states to be inserted are discarded; do not expand beyond dmax; enforce iteration budget imax; these settings affect pass rates and must be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterministic baseline reporting note
rubrics_metrics.description: The tidy baseline is deterministic, so there is no point attempting a proof search more than once under identical settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report single-run counts for deterministic baselines and consider stochasticity only for nondeterministic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling for pretraining/compute when comparing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing models across formal systems, control for pretraining and compute: both models applied to different systems were pre-trained on WebMath and trained on system-specific dumps with comparable overall compute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed performance differences (e.g., much better on Lean than Metamath) should be interpreted in light of equivalent compute and different system affordances (e.g., availability of high-level tactics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for access to high-level tactics in cross-system comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to high-level tactics can dramatically affect achievable performance; systems exposing powerful tactics (Lean) can show much higher pass rates than low-level systems (Metamath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comparisons and interpret results acknowledging whether systems provide tactic-level automation; generative models may need to produce arguments/premises to guide these tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset extensibility / porting encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: Porting effort: miniF2F currently targets Metamath, Lean, Isabelle, HOL Light and is eager to extend coverage to Coq and other systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions to extend formalizations and add support for more systems are welcomed to improve coverage (e.g., geometry, combinatorics) and cross-system comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark limitations should be disclosed: skewed coverage towards algebra/number theory/inequalities may bias research direction; some problem types are less covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note plan to extend coverage and encourage community contributions to address these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated formalization and review effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical estimate: for trained practitioners, formalizing a statement takes about 15 minutes on average, and reviewing a formalized statement about half of that on average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps estimate community effort required to expand or maintain the benchmark.
